This would be done by validating the incoming pointer msg and length before memcpy, and gracefully returning if invalid. A conservative approach would be to return early if msg is NULL or len == 0. A stronger guard would attempt to validate that msg points to readable memory within the VM’s memory pool. We should implement a safe, minimal guard (msg == NULL or len == 0) and, if feasible with the codebase, bounds-check msg against the pool boundaries. This change would prevent any accidental dereference of an invalid address from any code path calling njs_chb_append0, not only Array.prototype.join.
  2) Strengthen array join path: instead of passing raw string.start/string.size directly to njs_chb_append0, funnel through a safe helper that first validates the value is a well-formed string (e.g., via conversion/normalization).   3) If possible, add a runtime check within the join logic to ensure every element is converted to a valid string before appending; if not, skip or replace with a safe placeholder. This is more invasive, but significantly reduces risk.
- Recommended minimal fix now: implement a defensive check inside njs_chb_append0 as described in option 1 and also extend the early NULL/zero-length guards for all call sites that ultimately reach njs_chb_append0. This keeps changes small and localized to the core buffer writer and the call sites, ensuring sanitizer-driven crashes are avoided across all join/serialization paths.

  2) Build and run secb build; then run secb repro to verify sanitizer no longer reports a crash.
  3) If the crash persists, implement option 2 by wrapping append calls in Array.prototype.join with a helper that validates the string and falls back to an empty string when invalid.
